epigraph.text: Real life solutions of differential equations are not always highly differentiable, some are not differentiable at all, and some are not even continuous.
epigraph.by: Chapter 6, on why weak solutions exist

cards.q: What is the weak formulation of −ü = f with u(0)=u(1)=0, and what does it buy you?
cards.a:
Multiply by a test function v ∈ C₀∞([0,1]) (vanishes at the endpoints) and integrate by parts twice:
(f, v) = −(u, v̈)   for all such v.
This is the weak / variational form. It only needs fv and uv̈ integrable — u need not be C², continuous, or even a function.

The classical ODE is recovered when u is smooth enough. The point is the extra solutions: a curling wave is not a graph, but it can still be a weak solution.

r.rot: instead of asking u to have a second derivative (that's a lot of aura to demand), ask that against every smooth bump that dies at the ends, the inner product of f with the bump equals minus u against the bump's second derivative. integration by parts yeeted the derivatives onto the test function. now u can be rough, or not even a function, and the equation still makes sense. dumb-dumb: you stopped asking the solution to be pretty and started asking it to pass a vibe check against every nice test bump.
r.ex: The model problem −ü = f on (0,1) with Dirichlet ends is (6.1). Same pattern later for Green's functions and finite elements.
r.why: It is the language of the rest of the chapter. Distributions, eigenfunctions, Sturm–Liouville, Green's functions and finite elements all live in this weak inner-product world, not in C².
r.math: (f,v)=−(u,v̈) ∀ v∈C₀<sup>∞</sup>. Needs integrability, not classical derivatives.

cards.q: Define a distribution and the Dirac delta. How is a weak derivative defined?
cards.a:
Test functions D(Ω) = C₀∞(Ω): smooth, compact support inside Ω (hence vanish with all derivatives at ∂Ω).

Def 6.1.4. A distribution is a continuous linear functional on D(Ω). Write v[φ]. Every u ∈ L¹loc gives one by φ ↦ (u,φ); the Dirac delta δ[φ] = φ(0) is a distribution that is not given by a locally integrable function.

Def 6.1.10 (weak derivative): (∂u/∂xk)[φ] = −u[∂φ/∂xk]. For genuine C¹ functions this matches the classical derivative by integration by parts — the minus sign is that boundary term vanishing.

r.rot: a distribution is 'what happens when you pair me with every smooth bump.' ordinary functions do this by integration (normal behavior). dirac is the evaluation-at-zero bump-counter: δ[φ] = φ(0). no actual function integrates to that. dirac is not a function. it's an NPC that only talks at x=0. to differentiate a distribution, pass the derivative onto the test function and flip the sign — the same integration by parts that defined the weak form. so derivatives became 'make the bump do the work.'
r.ex: Nota Bene 6.1.7: everyone writes δ(x) and ∫δ(x)φ(x)dx = φ(0) as if δ were a function. It isn't; the left-hand side is defined to mean the right.
r.why: Once derivatives live on the test function, you can talk about solutions that aren't differentiable. That is the whole point of the chapter's opening examples.

cards.q: Define eigenfunctions of a linear operator on a function space. What extra care does infinite dimension demand?
cards.a:
Def 6.2.4. Lφ = ωφ with φ ≠ 0 in the space S on which L acts: ω is an eigenvalue, φ an eigenfunction. Same sentence as in finite dimensions.

The catch: in infinite dimensions, L − ωI failing to be invertible does not automatically mean ω is an eigenvalue. Spectrum is larger than the set of eigenvalues; you have to actually produce φ.

Example 6.2.5: Lu = uxx with u(0)=0, ux(1)=0. Try erx, r²=ω, and the boundary conditions kill the exponential/hyperbolic cases, leaving a cosine/sine family with discrete ω < 0.

r.rot: same definition as matrices: L hits φ and gives a scalar times φ. that's an eigenfunction. the difference is you cannot just look at det(L−ωI)=0, because infinite dimensions are ohio. 'not invertible' does not mean there's a kernel. you have to actually produce φ. guess a form (exponentials for constant-coefficient), plug in the boundary conditions, and only some ω survive. the rest get ratio'd by the boundary.
r.ex: Theorem 6.2.10: self-adjoint L has real eigenvalues, and distinct eigenvalues have orthogonal eigenfunctions — the infinite-dimensional spectral theorem in miniature.
r.why: Boundary-value problems are eigenvalue problems. The rest of the chapter (SL, Green's, FEM) needs a basis of eigenfunctions the way finite-dimensional linear algebra needs a basis of eigenvectors.
r.math: Lφ=ωφ. Infinite-dim: not invertible ⇏ eigenvalue. Self-adjoint ⇒ real ω, orthogonal eigenspaces.

cards.q: Define a Sturm–Liouville problem. Why does every second-order ODE hide one?
cards.a:
Def 6.3.1. On a bounded [a,b],
Lu = (1/r)[ −(p u')' + q u ],   p>0, r>0, p,q ∈ C²
The regular SL problem is Lu = ω r u (weight r). Singular if p or r vanish, or the interval is unbounded.

Special case p=1, q=0, r=1: L = −d²/dx².

Prop 6.3.4. Any −A u'' − B u' + C u = ω u on [a,b] can be rewritten as an SL problem (Exercise 6.11) — multiply by the integrating factor that turns the first-derivative term into a divergence.

r.rot: second-order linear BVP in divergence form, with a weight. that's sturm–liouville. the textbook −u'' is the boring special case (tutorial SL). the punchline is that every second-order ODE can be massaged into this shape with an integrating factor, so the nice spectral theory isn't a niche — it's the general 1d story. every 1d linear villain was SL in a trench coat.
r.ex: Regular SL with Dirichlet or Neumann ends: eigenvalues are real, simple, bounded below, and the eigenfunctions form an orthogonal basis of the weighted L² space (Thm 6.3.9).
r.why: SL is the self-adjoint 1d operator. Green's functions and the Fredholm alternative in the next pages are its linear algebra.
r.math: Lu=(1/r)[-(pu')'+qu]. Regular: p,r>0 on compact [a,b]. Every 2nd-order ODE is SL after an integrating factor.

cards.q: State the Fredholm alternative for a regular SL operator.
cards.a:
Thm 6.3.12. For a regular SL operator with the usual boundary conditions, exactly one of the following holds for Lu = f:
  • Either 0 is not an eigenvalue, L is invertible, and there is a unique solution for every f;
  • or 0 is an eigenvalue, and Lu = f has a solution iff f is orthogonal to every eigenfunction for eigenvalue 0. In that case the solution is unique up to adding those eigenfunctions.

Same dichotomy as Ax = b in finite dimensions: unique solution vs. solvability conditions from the kernel.

r.rot: either the homogeneous problem has only the zero solution, and you can solve Lu=f for every f (unique, W, invertible), or it has a kernel, and f has to be orthogonal to that kernel or there's no solution. that's fredholm: infinite-dimensional linear algebra with the same yes/no as matrices. Ax=b lore, but the matrix is an operator. if 0 is an eigenvalue you cannot invert, same as a singular matrix. no cap it's the same tweet.
r.ex: The Green's function of the next section exists precisely in the first case (0 not an eigenvalue). If 0 is an eigenvalue you cannot invert L.
r.why: It tells you when a BVP is well-posed before you try to solve it, and it is the solvability test behind Green's functions.
r.math: Either 0∉σ(L) and L<sup>−1</sup> exists, or 0∈σ(L) and f ⊥ ker L is necessary and sufficient.

cards.q: What is a Green's function, and how do eigenfunctions produce one?
cards.a:
The Green's function G(x,θ) of L is the integral kernel of a right inverse:
L(G(x,·)) = δ(x−θ),   so u(x) = ∫ G(x,θ) f(θ) dθ solves Lu = f.
Analogy: G is to L as A+ is to a matrix A (AA+ = I). The Dirac delta is the identity kernel.

Prop 6.4.1. If {φn} is an orthonormal eigenbasis with Lφn = ωn φn and no ωn = 0, then

G(x,θ) = Σn φn(x) φn(θ) / ωn
Same formula as the spectral inverse of a diagonalizable matrix, A−1 = Σ vnvnT/λn.

r.rot: to invert L, find a kernel G so that hitting G with L in x gives a delta at θ. then integrating G against f is applying L<sup>−1</sup>. G is the 'what would the solution look like if the forcing was a click at θ.' if you own an orthonormal eigenbasis, write G as the sum of φ(x)φ(θ)/ω — the same spectral inverse you already know for matrices. zero eigenvalues block the inverse (fredholm said so). no eigen-zeroes, you get a green's function. eigen-zeroes, it's over, no inverse.
r.ex: Exercise 6.16: L = −d²/dx² on [0,1] with Neumann ends. Constant functions are in the kernel, so no Green's function exists.
r.why: It turns 'solve the BVP' into 'integrate against a kernel you compute once'. FEM in the next section is a different inverse: project onto a finite-dimensional subspace instead of summing the whole eigenbasis.

cards.q: What is the Ritz–Galerkin idea, and what makes finite elements a special case?
cards.a:
The true solution lives in an infinite-dimensional space V. Pick a finite-dimensional S = span{\phi;j} of easy functions (not necessarily a subspace of V) and seek uS ∈ S close to u. That is Ritz–Galerkin.

Finite elements are RG with a piecewise-polynomial basis supported on a mesh. In 1D the model basis is hat functions: φi(xi)=1, φi(xj)=0 for j≠i, linear in between. Small support ⇒ sparse stiffness matrix. S is the continuous piecewise-linear functions that kink only at the nodes.

Unlike Ch 4's finite differences (values at nodes), FEM produces a function on the whole interval.

r.rot: don't approximate the derivative — approximate the space the solution lives in. pick a cheap finite-dimensional subspace, solve the weak form there. that's ritz–galerkin. finite elements are RG with tents: hat functions that are 1 at one node, 0 at the others, linear in between. because each hat only sees its two neighbours, the matrix is sparse (not fully cooked, just a few bands). unlike finite differences (numbers at nodes), FEM gives you an actual function on the whole interval. dumb-dumb: build the answer out of little tents.
r.ex: Model BVP: −u''=f on (0,1) with mixed ends. Weak form on S, existence/uniqueness in any finite-dimensional S ⊂ the energy space (Thm 6.5.4). The FEM solution is the best approximation in S in the energy norm (Thm 6.5.10).
r.why: It is how weak solutions become a numerical method. The same inner-product form that defined distributions now produces a linear system you can actually solve.
r.math: RG: solve the weak form in finite-dim S. FEM: S = piecewise polynomials on a mesh. Hats ⇒ sparse stiffness.
